title: JavaScript Async Handbook: Event Loop, Promises and async/await
summary: Quick revision notes on how JavaScript schedules work: the call stack, task and microtask queues, timer ordering, promises, async/await, error handling and the Promise combinators.

chapters.title: Event Loop Mental Model
points: JS runs one call stack on a single thread; a function runs to completion before anything else runs
Web APIs (timers, fetch, DOM events) do the waiting outside the stack and hand a callback to a queue when ready
Task queue (macrotasks) holds setTimeout, setInterval, I/O and UI event callbacks; microtask queue holds promise reactions, queueMicrotask and MutationObserver
Event loop rule: run one task, then drain the entire microtask queue, then render if needed, then pick the next task
Blocking the stack with a long synchronous loop freezes timers, clicks and rendering because nothing can be dequeued

chapters.title: Execution Order and setTimeout
points: Order of a script: synchronous code first, then all microtasks, then the next timer task
setTimeout(fn, 0) is not immediate: it queues a task after the current stack and all microtasks, and browsers clamp nested timers to about 4ms
Microtasks queued by microtasks run in the same drain, so an endless microtask chain starves timers and rendering
Classic trace: console.log('A'); setTimeout(()=>log('T')); Promise.resolve().then(()=>log('P')); log('B') prints A, B, P, T
Timers with equal delay fire in the order they were scheduled; the delay is a minimum, not a guarantee

chapters.title: Promises and async/await
points: A promise is in one of three states: pending, fulfilled or rejected; it settles once and its value never changes
then(onOk, onErr) returns a new promise; returning a value fulfils it, returning a promise adopts it, throwing rejects it
Callbacks passed to then/catch/finally always run as microtasks, even if the promise is already settled
An async function always returns a promise; await pauses only that function and schedules the rest as a microtask when the awaited promise settles
await in a loop runs steps sequentially; start the promises first and await them together to run in parallel: const [a,b] = await Promise.all([f(),g()])

chapters.title: Error Handling Patterns
points: A rejected promise skips every then until a catch; catch returns a fulfilled promise, so the chain continues after it
In async functions use try/catch around await; finally runs on both success and failure
An unhandled rejection raises the unhandledrejection event in browsers and crashes Node 15+ by default
Forgetting to return or await a promise inside then/async makes its error escape the chain and go unhandled
new Promise(executor) turns a throw inside the executor into a rejection, but a throw inside a later setTimeout callback is not caught by it

chapters.title: Promise.all, allSettled, race and any
points: Promise.all: fulfils with an array of values in input order, rejects immediately on the first rejection
Promise.allSettled: never rejects, fulfils with [{status:'fulfilled',value}|{status:'rejected',reason}] for every input
Promise.race: settles with the first promise to settle, whether it fulfils or rejects; used for timeouts
Promise.any: fulfils with the first fulfilment, ignores rejections, and rejects with AggregateError only if all reject
Combinators do not cancel the losing promises; their work keeps running

chapters.title: Async Cheat Sheet
points: Order: sync code, then microtasks (promise.then, await continuation, queueMicrotask), then timers and I/O tasks
Combinator pick: all = need every result, allSettled = need every outcome, race = first to finish, any = first success
Sequential loop: for (const x of xs) await f(x); parallel: await Promise.all(xs.map(f))
Always return or await promises and attach a catch; forEach with an async callback does not wait
Timeout pattern: Promise.race([work, new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(() => rej(new Error('timeout')), ms))])
